title: Exploring designers' finishing materials selection for residential interior spaces
research_focus: To explore the determinants of materials selection in interior design, identify designers' finishing material preferences and selection criteria for floors, walls, and ceilings in residential contexts, and investigate designers' criteria prioritizations.

sample_context.description: 16 interior designers and 14 architects specializing in residential projects, based in Ankara, Turkey, aged 35–56 years with a minimum of 10 years of experience.
sample_context.setting: Participants' architectural/interior design offices, discussing actual residential projects and a simulated residential entry hall.

findings.antecedent: Material properties (technical, sensorial, intangible, ecological, manufacturing) and market properties (cost, availability, skilled workmanship)
findings.description: Designers' material choices are strongly influenced by the intrinsic properties of materials (durability, aesthetics, meaning, health, manufacturability) and market factors like cost, availability, and the need for skilled labor.
supporting_quotes: I take particular care to select hard (MRD; Mat-Technical) material where the circulation is high (PRD; Function).
I love to add texture to my projects (MRD; Mat-Sensorial).
It is very important that a material does not harm human health (MRD; Mat-Ecological).
In the market, we cannot reach the people who apply this material properly.

findings.antecedent: Project's physical aspects (site, layout, existing surfaces), functional considerations, client requests, and budget
findings.description: Material selection is shaped by the project's physical context (e.g., existing building characteristics, narrow corridors), functional requirements (e.g., ease of cleaning, durability for circulation), client aesthetic and economic preferences, and budgetary constraints.
supporting_quotes: It was an old building, so the corridors are really narrow (PRD; Physical).
My considerations on materials change according to the function this material will be used for (PRD; Function).
The customer's tastes are particularly decisive in residential projects...
I like marble more (DRD; Design approach), but unfortunately, it is an expensive material (MRD; Cost).

findings.antecedent: Designers' material knowledge (indirectly acquired from sources, directly acquired from experience) and personal design approach (preferences, values, conceptual principles)
findings.description: Designers' choices are influenced by their accumulated knowledge from various sources (websites, samples, past projects) and their individual design philosophy, aesthetic preferences, and conceptual intentions for the space.
supporting_quotes: I tried to use materials that I know. I mean ... There are some material suppliers that we collaborate with.
When choosing the materials, I take into account the information I have acquired from my previous experiences.
I personally love (DRD; Design approach) using the same material for the whole circulation area because it shows the space as larger than it is.

findings.antecedent: Residential project context (actual vs. simulated without client/budget constraints)
findings.description: In actual projects, ceramic (34%), wood (31%), and marble (26%) were top choices. In simulated projects (no constraints), marble (32%) and granite (18%) preference increased, while ceramic (16%) and wood (16%) decreased, and a wider variety of materials were chosen, indicating less concern for cost.

findings.antecedent: Residential project context (actual vs. simulated without client/budget constraints)
findings.description: Paint (34% actual, 23% simulated), wallpaper (27% actual, 19% simulated), and wood (25% actual, 23% simulated) were top choices in both contexts. Simulated projects showed a wider variety of wall finishes, with increased use of marble (10% vs 6%) and mirrors (13% vs 2%), and additional use of exposed concrete and epoxy.

findings.antecedent: Residential project context (actual vs. simulated without client/budget constraints)
findings.description: Paint (82% actual, 69% simulated) and wood (9% actual, 14% simulated) were the most frequently chosen ceiling materials in both actual and simulated projects, with a narrower range of materials selected compared to floors or walls. Simulated projects showed slightly more variety.

findings.antecedent: Interior surface (floor, wall, ceiling) and design context (actual vs. simulated)
findings.consequent: Number and variety of finishing materials used, interrelation of material choices
findings.source: Results - Materials preferences and selection criteria
findings.description: Designers often chose more than one material per surface, with a greater variety and combinations observed in the simulated project (e.g., 77% of walls had at least two materials in simulated vs. 43% in actual). Decisions for one surface were made in relation to others, aiming for atmospheric effects and textural balance.
supporting_quotes: The wood on the floor is used to separate the circulation route from the entry hall subspace, which is granite. The use of natural stone and wood with wallpaper is to preserve the asymmetric balance of the opposite wall. The ceiling has hidden lighting fixtures with spray plaster and paint to maintain textural balance.

findings.antecedent: Finishing material selection for walls, floors, and ceilings (simulated project)
findings.description: Designers prioritized sensorial properties (color, texture, smell, sound) most highly across all surfaces (M=4.57 floors, M=4.83 walls, M=4.20 ceilings), with walls receiving the highest sensorial priority due to their visual attention-grabbing potential.

findings.antecedent: Finishing material selection for walls, floors, and ceilings (simulated project)
findings.description: Technical properties (durability, strength, conductivity, density) were the second highest priority for designers across all surfaces (M=4.23 floors, M=4.00 walls, M=3.93 ceilings).

findings.antecedent: Finishing material selection for walls, floors, and ceilings (simulated project)
findings.description: Ecological properties (recyclability, sustainability, non-toxicity) were given the lowest priority across all surfaces (M=2.90 floors, M=2.93 walls, M=2.97 ceilings), despite designers claiming their importance in interviews, suggesting a gap between stated values and actual practice.

findings.antecedent: Finishing material selection for walls, floors, and ceilings (simulated project)
findings.description: Intangible properties (emotions, meanings, culture, trends) were prioritized in the mid-range (M=3.70 floors, M=3.83 walls, M=3.33 ceilings), with walls receiving higher priority than floors and ceilings.

findings.antecedent: Finishing material selection for walls, floors, and ceilings (simulated project)
findings.description: Manufacturing properties (ease of manufacture, assembly, finishing techniques) were prioritized in the mid-range (M=3.77 floors, M=3.77 walls, M=3.93 ceilings), with slightly higher scores for ceilings than for walls and floors.

derived_hypotheses: The interplay of material selection criteria changes in importance over the course of the design and material selection process.
Design approaches differ based on demographic characteristics (age, gender, professional background, practice experience).
The freedom from client and budgetary constraints in simulated projects leads to a greater variety and number of material choices compared to actual projects.
Designers' stated importance of ecological properties will diverge from their actual prioritization in practice.
mechanism_candidates: Designers' reliance on direct experiential knowledge and skilled workmanship for material choice influences their selection decisions.
The holistic nature of interior space leads designers to make material decisions for one surface in relation to others, aiming for overall atmospheric effects.
The visual attention-grabbing potential of walls drives higher prioritization of sensorial properties for this surface.
The lack of tactile component and direct visual field for ceilings leads to lower prioritization of sensorial properties for this surface.
transferability_limits: Findings are limited to the Turkish context, where cultural and geographical factors (material intangible properties, cost, market availability) may vary.
The study sample is restricted to experienced architects and interior designers, potentially yielding different results with newly graduated designers or those with different professional expertise.
The study did not focus on end-user preferences, which could influence material selections.
Findings are specific to residential entry hall typology and may not apply to other building types or scales due to varying functional and project-related determinants.
limitations: Restricted number of architects and interior designers with sufficient relevant experience as participants.
Did not focus on end-user preferences.
